Deliverable 05 · reflection

What the data supports—and what it cannot prove

Expanding from a hand-selected sample to all 103 official records made the project much stronger—but it also clarified the boundary between a facilities inventory and student experience.

The evidence supports

Comparison

  • The official directory contains 103 named spaces across 13 libraries and 2,098 listed seats.
  • Lamont and Widener together account for 47% of listed capacity.
  • Silent or Whispers settings and Chatter settings form meaningfully different options for students.
  • Reservability and collaboration equipment vary enough to guide a facilities audit.
  • Task-specific rankings communicate trade-offs more honestly than one universal “best space” list.

The evidence cannot prove

Experience

  • Which space students actually like most or rate most highly.
  • How crowded a room will be at a particular time.
  • Whether an unlisted amenity is absent or merely undocumented.
  • Whether the official directory covers every Harvard study environment.
  • Whether adding an amenity would cause better grades, wellbeing, or library use.

I would improve the project by pairing the official inventory with two privacy-preserving sources: periodic anonymous occupied-seat counts by broad time block and a short intercept survey asking students to rank features and rate broad space types. That would separate “what is published,” “what exists,” “what is in demand,” and “what students experience.” Until then, the dashboard should be read as a transparent decision aid and a facilities-data audit—not as a definitive ranking.
